steps.title: Load PVT cell with CO2
steps.instruction: Fill the high‑pressure PVT‑cell with CO₂ from a cylinder via a pump, set the pump to the required pressure (e.g., 50 bar) and maintain this pressure throughout the experiment; set the cell temperature (e.g., 25 °C) and keep it constant using a NiCr‑Ni thermocouple.

steps.title: Create n‑decane pendant drop
steps.instruction: After the cell reaches the target pressure and temperature, generate a pendant drop of n‑decane (the drop phase, Pd) at the tip of the capillary tube inside the cell.

steps.title: Start image capture
steps.instruction: Immediately activate the high‑resolution camera and the ADVANCE image‑analysis software to begin recording digital images of the pendant drop for later volume analysis.

steps.title: Monitor diffusion to equilibrium
steps.instruction: Allow CO₂ (environmental phase, Pg) to diffuse into the n‑decane drop; continue the experiment until the pendant‑drop volume shows no or only minimal increase, indicating equilibrium (example: equilibrium reached at 50 bar, 25 °C).

steps.title: Determine pendant drop volume over time
steps.instruction: Using the captured images and the image‑analysis software, measure the pendant‑drop volume (VPd) at each time point from t = 0 (pure n‑decane) onward.

substeps.instruction: Import each image into the software.
Apply the pendant‑drop analysis algorithm to obtain VPd for that frame.

steps.title: Calculate CO₂ volume in drop
steps.instruction: For each time point, compute the CO₂ volume inside the drop (VCO₂) by subtracting the known initial hydrocarbon volume (VHC, measured at t = 0) from the total pendant‑drop volume: VCO₂(t) = VPd(t) – VHC.

steps.title: Compute mole fractions of components
steps.instruction: Convert VCO₂ and VHC to masses using densities of CO₂ and n‑decane (ρCO₂, ρHC) obtained from the NIST Webbook at the experimental P,T; then calculate moles and mole fractions xCO₂ and xHC for each time point.

substeps.instruction: Mass_CO₂ = VCO₂ × ρCO₂; Mass_HC = VHC × ρHC.
Moles_CO₂ = Mass_CO₂ / MolarMass_CO₂; Moles_HC = Mass_HC / MolarMass_HC.

steps.title: Calculate pendant drop density
steps.instruction: Determine the density of the binary pendant drop (ρPd) at each time using the mixture rule: ρPd(t) = xCO₂(t)·ρCO₂ + xHC(t)·ρHC, where ρCO₂ and ρHC are the pure‑component densities at the experimental pressure and temperature.

steps.title: Obtain interfacial tension from software
steps.instruction: Enter the time‑dependent pendant‑drop density values into the ADVANCE software (or equivalent) to compute the dynamic interfacial tension (IFT) at each time point and the equilibrium IFT once the volume no longer changes.

substeps.instruction: Load the density series into the software.
Run the pendant‑drop shape analysis to extract IFT versus time.
Record both the dynamic IFT profile and the final equilibrium IFT.

description: Interfacial tension plays a significant role in numerous engineering applications involving multiphase flow. Measuring the IFT is a crucial part of multiphase systems, there are several methods available like ring method, drop volume method, spinning drop method, bubble pressure method and pendant drop method. In recent years, the pendant drop method has been widely used as an effective method with high accuracy (±0.05 mN/m2) [1,2], especially at elevated pressure and temperature. There are several types of equipment available that rely on pendant drop method to estimate the IFT, few of them are IFT-700 (Vinci Technologies), IFT-10-P (Core laboratories), DSA-00 (KRÜSS), and Model-190 (ramé-hart instrument). Most of these use image processing combined with Young-Laplace equation to estimate the IFT. The primary difficulty associated with IFT measurement by pendant drop mechanism is providing the appropriate densities of the two phases, especially in a system consisting of gas (like CO2, methane, and propane) and liquids (water and hydrocarbon). Multiphase systems like CO2-hydrocarbon, CO2-water/brine, and carbonated water-hydrocarbon are of increasing interest due to their application in petroleum (CO2 EOR), environmental (CO2 sequestration) and renewable energy (geothermal). When CO2 contact liquid (hydrocarbon) it diffuses and dissolves into the liquids, forming a binary mixture. The diffusion of gases into liquids alters the composition of the resulting binary mixture, hence alter the properties like density. Obtaining the density of the binary mixture is complex, especially at elevated pressures and temperatures and as a function of time. Most of the studies have neglected the density changes due to the solubility effects of dissolved gases in bulk liquids and have used the density of pure fluids instead of the binary mixture [3,4].
